title: Stereochemical Redundancy Inflates Benchmark Performance of Two-Dimensional Molecular Representations in Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability Prediction
content: Background: Machine learning models for blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability are routinely benchmarked on the B3DB dataset, with reported areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) frequently exceeding 0.90. Scaffold-based data splitting is widely regarded as sufficient protection against optimistic bias. We hypothesised that this protection is incomplete, because the two-dimensional (2D) molecular representations in general use cannot distinguish stereoisomers, which therefore remain effectively duplicated across scaffold-disjoint partitions. Methods: B3DB (7,807 records) was curated under two strategies: conventional deduplication on canonical SMILES and deduplication on the InChIKey skeleton, which collapses stereoisomers, tautomers, and protonation variants. Under each curation we evaluated five models, a physicochemical-descriptor logistic regression baseline, ECFP4 random forest, ECFP4 XGBoost, ECFP4 LightGBM, and a combined ECFP4-plus-descriptor LightGBM, across 20 independent randomized Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits. Probability calibration and classification thresholds were derived exclusively from validation partitions. Uncertainty was quantified by bootstrap and paired across-split comparison. An applicability domain analysis stratified test compounds by maximum Tanimoto similarity to training chemistry. A dedicated experiment assessed whether chirality-aware fingerprints could resolve skeletons carrying discordant labels. Results: Canonical-SMILES deduplication identified only 3 duplicate structures. Skeleton-level deduplication identified 1,490 duplicated skeletons, reducing the dataset from 7,802 to 3,952 compounds, and revealed 131 skeletons carrying discordant BBB+/BBB− labels. Apparent performance fell substantially under skeleton-collapsed curation: ECFP4 random forest from ROC-AUC 0.938 ± 0.025 to 0.871 ± 0.033, and the descriptor baseline from 0.851 ± 0.021 to 0.782 ± 0.030. The inflation was therefore comparable for fingerprint and descriptor representations (0.062 to 0.070 and 0.069 ROC-AUC, respectively), indicating a representation-general rather than fingerprint-specific artifact. The advantage of fingerprints over physicochemical descriptors was robust to curation (paired ΔROC-AUC 0.091, 95% CI 0.065 to 0.119 and 0.093 ± 0.033, favoring fingerprints in 20 of 20 splits). Performance depended steeply on chemical proximity to training data, with ROC-AUC rising from 0.723 for compounds lacking any close training analogue to 0.935 for those with one. All 131 discordant skeletons were genuine stereoisomer pairs; although 126 (96.2%) were distinguishable by chirality-aware fingerprints, such fingerprints ordered discordant pairs correctly in only 66 of 131 cases (50.4%, chance level). Conclusions: Skeleton-level redundancy in B3DB inflates benchmark performance of all common 2D representations by approximately 0.07 ROC-AUC, and scaffold splitting does not prevent this because stereoisomers share a scaffold-independent identity. We recommend skeleton-level deduplication as a mandatory curation step and routine reporting of applicability-domain-stratified performance. Stereochemically determined label conflicts are real and irreducible for 2D methods, placing an intrinsic ceiling on achievable accuracy.
